analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 221-210 in June 2023 with only 1 Democrat in favor, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, federal agencies write and enforce regulations that carry out laws Congress passes — on things like clean air, workplace safety, and consumer finance. This bill would flip that: any rule the government classifies as "major" (generally one with an economic effect of $100 million a year or more) could not take effect unless both chambers of Congress passed, and the president signed, a resolution specifically approving that rule. If Congress did nothing for 70 session days, the rule would simply die. The House version also required agencies to send 20% of their existing rules to Congress each year for five years for review; any rule Congress did not affirmatively approve within 90 days would lose its force, and unapproved rules would eventually expire.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that face costly regulations would gain the most: instead of needing to defeat a rule once through an agency, they could ask a single chamber of a divided Congress to kill it by simply never voting. Supporters also argue every voter gains accountability, because the elected Congress — not unelected agency staff — would have to sign off on the most consequential rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated businesses facing costly federal rules

how_it_helps.text: A "major rule" — one with an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, a major increase in costs or prices for consumers or industries, or significant effects on competition, employment, or investment — could take effect only if Congress passed a joint resolution of approval that the president signed.
If such a resolution was not enacted within 70 session days, the rule would be deemed not approved and could not take effect, so a single chamber could kill any major rule by inaction.

The House-passed version added a review process for existing rules: each agency would designate at least 20% of its rules for review annually over five years, and any designated rule Congress did not approve within 90 days would have no effect; five years after enactment, eligible rules never affirmatively approved would sunset.

Supporters framed the bill as restoring constitutional accountability, arguing Congress has excessively delegated lawmaking to executive agencies and should vote on the most consequential rules itself.
The bill preserved fast-track procedures requiring committees to be discharged and votes to be held within fixed deadlines, so approval resolutions could not be buried in committee.

analysis.who_pays: The public relies on agency rules for protections Congress does not itself write — clean air and water limits, workplace and food safety standards, drug safety, and consumer financial protections. Under this bill, those protections above the $100 million threshold would need an affirmative vote in a politically divided Congress to exist at all, and the House version threatened to wipe out existing rules that Congress failed to re-approve. Regulated industries would gain a veto point they could target at each individual rule.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through weakened federal protections

drawbacks.text: Because approval requires action by both chambers and a presidential signature, major rules would regularly fail by default in divided government, leaving agencies unable to carry out laws Congress has already passed on public health, safety, and the environment.

The House version's review of existing rules put current protections at risk: designated rules not approved by Congress within 90 days would have no effect, and rules never affirmatively approved would expire after five years.
The bill barred courts from reviewing most determinations under the new process, limiting oversight of how rules were classified and handled.

Even many supporters would acknowledge the mechanism is blunt: it treats all rules above the $100 million threshold the same, whether the rule protects against pollution, fraud, or unsafe products, and substitutes one political filter for case-by-case rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is real — Congress does delegate enormous lawmaking power to agencies, and a vote requirement would force members to own the consequences. But the cost side is heavy: in divided government the mechanism amounts to a default repeal of new major protections, and the House version went further by putting existing rules in jeopardy of expiring unless a divided Congress affirmatively re-approved them one batch at a time. The bill's practical effect would be to shift power from public-protection agencies to regulated industries' allies in Congress, and the House's near-perfect party split suggests the accountability framing did not persuade anyone to cross party lines on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill in June 2023, but the Senate only read it and placed it on its calendar; no vote ever happened, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill as amended by a 13-5 vote on May 24, 2023.
The House passed the bill on June 14, 2023, by a vote of 221 to 210.
The vote was almost entirely along party lines: 220 of 221 Republicans voted yes, while 210 of 212 Democrats voted no and only 1 Democrat voted yes.
Before passage, a Democratic motion to recommit the bill to committee failed 210-220, with all 210 voting Democrats in favor and all 220 voting Republicans opposed.
The Senate received the bill on June 20, 2023, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders; no further action was ever taken.
The bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without a Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the bill — chiefly Senate Democrats who never allowed a vote — and the agencies and public-protection rules the bill targeted came out ahead: existing regulations remain in force and agencies can still issue major rules without congressional approval. Businesses hoping to gain a congressional veto over costly regulations gained nothing this time.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturing, energy, utilities, chemicals, finance)
industries.note: The bill would have given businesses facing major rules — the ones most likely to involve worker safety, pollution limits, and consumer protections — a new veto point: a single chamber of a divided Congress could kill any such rule by never voting on it. The House version's review-and-sunset process could also have forced existing rules to expire unless Congress affirmatively re-approved them.

Advocacy groups depend on agency rulemaking to turn public-protection statutes into enforceable standards; the bill would have made those standards hostage to congressional approval, so their position ran alongside the public's in this fight.
